newsitem.title: USA: Winter storm slams U.S. northern plains.
newsitem.headline: Winter storm slams U.S. northern plains.

text.p: A blizzard dumped up to three feet (a metre) of snow on parts of the northern plains on Sunday, temporarily halting the spring thaw that has turned rivers into lakes and forced scores of evacuations.
"This is the biggest blizzard of the season -- bigger than they had even over the winter," National Weather Service meteorologist Greg Carbin said.
Wind gusts of up to 60 miles per hour (100 km/h) created drifts as high as 10 feet (3 m), clogging roads from Wyoming to Minnesota.
Fargo, a city of 75,000 along the eastern border of North Dakota, was buried under a thick layer of snow. High winds caused drifting and cut visibility to only a few yards (metres).
In hard-hit North Dakota, freezing rain and sleet turned to snow overnight on Saturday, but not before coating trees and power lines that knocked out electricity in some areas.

Three temporary dikes erected to hold back the rising Red River in the southeast corner of the state in Wahpeton collapsed late on Saturday under a steady downpour, forcing 30 families to leave their homes, authorities said.

Towns along the Red River and its tributaries, as well as hamlets in southwestern Minnesota, have been fighting floodwaters for the past week, building dikes and sandbag walls. The mixture of rain and snow and the arrival of colder weather made the work miserable.
But the snowstorm and its accompanying sub-freezing temperatures put a temporary halt to the spring thaw that has inundated towns in the Dakotas, Minnesota, and Wisconsin.
"This might ease some of the flood threat. But now the snow is as deep again as it was before it started melting," the Weather Service's Carbin said. "This just adds insult to injury."
Temperatures were not expected to climb above freezing across much of the region until the end of the week at the earliest, he said.
